title: Domains and the right sign-in context
description: Understand how subdomains separate login namespaces without confusing them with operational projects.

chapters.title: The address helps choose the context

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Imagine a fictional provider operating Hub for two customers. Each has a colleague named Alex. How can the platform keep those sign-in identities in the right context?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The domains feature adds a login namespace selected through a subdomain. Each customer can have its own context, so the same visible username can exist in different domains. The address you open helps Hub know which domain you're signing into.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So Alex should pay attention to the login page, not just type a familiar username?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Yes. The login page shows the domain, and the profile shows a domain badge after sign-in. Those are useful checks when an account appears to be missing or a login works in one address but not another.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Is this simply another name for selecting a project?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: No. Keep the concepts separate. This guide is about the domain used for account sign-in. Organisation and project selection describe a different working context. Don't assume that changing a login address transfers cameras or changes the permissions a user holds.

chapters.title: Enable it as a deployment feature

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can our provider just invent a new address and expect the right account to appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The deployment must enable the feature and configure its base domain. The guide explains how the subdomain becomes the selected Hub domain. Account names are internally associated with that domain, while people still use their regular visible username at sign-in.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What happens to subaccounts created by a customer account?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The guide says they're added to the same domain and linked to their master account. Before enabling the feature, work out which customer addresses and account contexts you intend to use. Then verify a sign-in and the visible domain badge.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: A clear address, a clear domain badge, and no guessing which Alex we mean. The linked guide has the exact deployment settings.

editorialStyle.tone: A short, high-level introduction for a first-time listener. Explain why the topic matters, build one mental model, and suggest one next action. Sound like two colleagues, not a narrated manual.
editorialStyle.scope: Aim for four to five minutes and roughly 500-550 spoken words. Use one fictional example and four short chapters. Leave identifiers, form limits, configuration, migration mechanics, and troubleshooting checklists in the linked guide. Keep essential caveats as practical consequences.
editorialStyle.humour: Optional: one or two brief, relevant light moments are enough. Prefer a relatable analogy over a separate joke. Never pad the overview with banter.
editorialStyle.reactions: Use occasional short, natural responses such as 'Oh, that makes sense' or 'Wait, so...' followed by a real question. Avoid repetitive praise, canned agreement, and filler.
editorialStyle.laughter: Optional: at most one or two light reactions such as 'Ha, fair point.' Never insert [laughs], SSML, or repeated ha-ha strings. These are spoken reactions, not a guarantee of genuine laughter from the current speech engine.
editorialStyle.intonation: Write real questions with question marks, use contractions, alternate short and longer sentences, and make contrasts explicit. Let punctuation and sentence rhythm suggest curiosity, surprise, and emphasis. Avoid all-caps shouting, excessive exclamation marks, and artificial pause tags.
editorialStyle.guardrails: Keep technical claims source-backed. Never mock the listener, joke about real victims, minimize security or data-loss risks, or let humour replace an explanation. Personality is optional; accuracy and clarity are not.
